bib.title: If You Want Coherence, Orchestrate a Team of Rivals: Multi-Agent Models of Organizational Intelligence

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "If You Want Coherence, Orchestrate a Team of Rivals: Multi-Agent Models of Organizational Intelligence". Vijayaraghavan, Jayachandran, Murthy, Govindan, Subramanian (all Isotopes AI, USA, a vendor). arXiv 2601.14351v1 [cs.MA], 20 Jan 2026, preprint. The format is ACM-style, but I saw no venue.

COVERAGE: I extracted all 15 pages (80,609 chars) and read the abstract, intro, related work, architecture, evaluation, discussion, limitations, conclusion, and the start of the references. I read §3.2–3.4 only by keyword search, not line by line. Those sections cover the message-passing kernel, Context Ray Tracing and the planner/executor pipeline. The extraction was clean.

CORE CLAIM: Reliability comes from organisation, not from a better single agent. Planners, executors and critics hold strict roles and opposing incentives. Critics have hierarchical veto, not a vote, and check against acceptance criteria declared in advance. The paper calls this "errors should die in committee". Tool and data calls run in a remote code executor, so raw data stays out of agent context. Only schemas and summaries return.

HEADLINE NUMBERS
1. Production sessions: 522 sessions, all financial-analysis tasks. 130 (24.9%) passed first time. 344 were recovered by the inner loop (Code Critique 337, Chart Critique 7). Output Critique saved 7 more. 41 (7.9%) were rejected by users. Overall success was 92.1% (481/522).
   - The paper says the baseline error rate was 75%, which matches 24.9% clean first pass.
   - There is no control arm on those same 522 sessions. "Success" means the user did not disapprove.
2. Controlled comparison: one task, 9 invoices against a QuickBooks Online (QBO) expense report, with a $40 ground-truth discrepancy.
   - Single agent: 10 trials, 60% correct. 30% gave a wrong amount and 10% said "no discrepancy". It was confident in all 10.
   - Self-verify ("please verify your reconciliation"): 5 trials. 3 flipped from correct to incorrect, 2 stayed correct.
   - Multi-agent: 20 trials, 90% (18/20), 4.2 min against 1–2 min.
   - The single-agent model is only "a frontier model from a leading vendor". The paper names no model for either arm.
3. Cost: recovery added 38.6% of credits and 21.8% of active time, measured over the 392 sessions that needed recovery. Level 3 sessions are 28% of sessions but 68% of recovery credits. 40% of sessions (157/392) recovered in 1–2 extra iterations for 19.6% of credits.
4. Case study: 8-step plan, 13 critique iterations, 5 automatic retries, 12.8 min, 88.89% match (8 of 9 invoices).

ABLATION
- There is no true ablation. There is a layer-by-layer catch analysis: Code Critique catches 86.0% of errors in the sessions that reach it, Chart Critique 1.8%, Output Critique 14.6% of the 48 that reached it.
- Code and Chart critics never overlapped (385 and 7 sessions, mutually exclusive). The authors call this support for orthogonal critics.
- A hypothetical fourth critic as effective as Output Critique would cut the escape rate only from 7.9% to 6.7% (6 sessions). This is projected, not tested.
- No run removes the planner, uses a same-model critic, or compares veto against voting.

QUOTES
- "Sub-agents cannot see sibling work. When one sub-agent assumes fiscal year ends in December and another assumes March, the parent receives conflicting outputs with no visibility into the conflicting assumptions." (p4, §3.1.2; it cites Cognition's "actions carry implicit decisions")
- "Self-verification reduced accuracy rather than improving it. The same reasoning process that produced the initial answer cannot reliably evaluate it." (p13)
- "Agents write code; Jupyter executes against real data; only schemas and summaries return to context." (p9, §3.5.1)
- "Critics run on different models than writers for cognitive diversity, not self-review." (p9)

LIMITS
- Authors concede: finance only; cost at scale; sequential latency from each critic layer; a 7% floor (93% as the practical ceiling); and no false-positive measurement for critics. They also concede the baselines are "illustrative rather than exhaustive".
- Not shown:
  - Any benchmark or public dataset.
  - Confidence intervals. n=10 and n=20 are tiny.
  - A same-model critic against a different-model critic. The "cognitive diversity" claim is asserted, not tested.
  - The context-firewall benefit measured on its own.
  - Named models or dollar costs. Cost is in unitless "credits".
  - Anything about the "50+ agents" beyond design.
  - Reproducibility. The transcripts are only a tinyurl link.
- The 522-session "success" is judged by user approval, not ground truth.
- The cost of the multi-agent design is inference calls: "multiply inference calls".
- It argues against naive fan-out for non-independent subtasks, but it never tests it. Its comparison is a single agent against a critic council, not against sub-agents.

BUILDS ON (as printed in its references)
- Cemri et al. 2025, MAST failure taxonomy, arXiv:2503.13657 (14 failure modes, 1,600+ traces).
- Huang et al., faulty-agent resilience (Challenger and Inspector), 2024.
- Cognition's analysis [4] of naive multi-agent failure.
- Anthropic's multi-agent research system [1].
- ReAct [15].
- Raza et al. 2025, TRiSM, arXiv:2506.04133.
- Shannon 1948 (the noisy-channel framing).
- The Swiss-cheese model.
- The remote code executor, citing [7]. I did not check what [7] is.

FIT FOR NOTE 07
Moderate to weak as evidence, but useful as a vendor case study and a taxonomy.
- Usable for the generator/evaluator split and veto against voting.
- Usable for the context firewall (code execution returns only summaries).
- Usable for the "why not naive sub-agents" argument (§3.1.2, Table 1).
- Usable for the diminishing-returns point on extra critics.
- Usable for the cost: about 40% overhead and 2–3x latency.
- Its best fit is note 05 (verification loops): self-verification degrades accuracy, and the critic catch-rate table.
- Do not cite 90% against 60% as a general result. It is one task, with unnamed models and tiny n.

FIGURE CANDIDATE
Figure 4 (p11): the session recovery flow for 522 sessions (130 clean, 344 inner loop, 7 output, 41 rejected). It shows layered catch faster than prose. I did not extract the caption list with the figures script, so check the figure itself before using it.

PROBLEMS: none. The text contained no embedded instructions.
